---
title: "Zeros in count data"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

More observed zeros than a Poisson model predicts do not by themselves establish a separate zero-generating process. We examine this ambiguity with the data from Storme's ([2024](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11525-024-09429-8)) French liaison study. One row is a final-morpheme, final-consonant, and liaison-status combination. Following Storme's analysis, the numerical response is the integer part of 100 times summed `freqfilms2`. We call it a **truncated frequency proxy** because it is derived from normalized frequency rather than counted liaison tokens with a known corpus exposure.

A spike at zero can come from the measurement rule, an ordinary one-process
distribution, or a genuinely separate state. Auditing how the released proxy
creates zeros is thus a prerequisite for deciding what either likelihood can
teach.

```{r}
#| label: load-storme-zero
#| echo: true
storme <- read.csv("data/storme-liaison/storme-liaison-counts.csv")
stopifnot(nrow(storme) == 11195L)
storme$liaison <- factor(storme$liaison, levels = c("no", "yes"))
storme$final_consonant <- factor(storme$final_consonant)
storme$truncated_frequency_proxy <- storme$reconstructed_count
```

Here is the first observed cell:

```{r}
#| label: inspect-one-storme-cell
storme[1L, c(
  "final_morpheme", "final_consonant", "liaison",
  "frequency_per_million_sum", "reconstructed_count"
)]
```

If $f_{h}$ denotes `freqfilms2` for row $h$ in a particular morpheme--consonant--liaison cell, the calculation is

$$
y
=
\operatorname{trunc}
\left(
100\sum_h f_h
\right).
$$

Algebraically, a positive sum below $.01$ would also become zero after the
transformation. The prepared values contain no such case: their smallest positive
sum is exactly $.01$, and every proxy zero corresponds to an exact zero summed
frequency. That empirical coincidence makes the zero/nonzero boundary stable in
this table. It does not turn the positive integers into observed token counts or
supply a count exposure and sampling process.

```{r}
#| label: audit-storme-frequency-proxy
data.frame(
  rows = nrow(storme),
  exact_zero_frequency = sum(storme$frequency_per_million_sum == 0),
  zero_truncated_proxy = sum(storme$truncated_frequency_proxy == 0),
  minimum_positive_frequency = min(
    storme$frequency_per_million_sum[storme$frequency_per_million_sum > 0]
  ),
  median_positive_frequency = median(
    storme$frequency_per_million_sum[storme$frequency_per_million_sum > 0]
  )
)
```

A measurement-aligned two-part analysis would model whether summed frequency is
zero and then model `frequency_per_million_sum` among positive cells. That target
concerns presence and the magnitude of a normalized frequency. It differs from a
negative-binomial token-count target and would require a declared continuous
positive distribution. The integer fits below are therefore likelihood stress
tests for this proxy, not preferred generative models of corpus tokens.

We fit additive Poisson and negative-binomial baselines with the same mean
formula. For both fits, the
[likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) holds the observed
proxy values fixed and compares parameter values under the declared response
distribution. The negative binomial allows

$$
\operatorname{Var}[Y_i\mid\mu_i]=\mu_i+\frac{\mu_i^2}{\theta},
$$

so ordinary heterogeneity can increase both tails, including zero mass.

A zero-inflated count model would instead introduce a second process. With structural-zero probability $\omega_i$ and count mean $\mu_i$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=0)
=
\omega_i+(1-\omega_i)f_{\text{count}}(0\mid\mu_i),
$$

and for $y>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=y)
=(1-\omega_i)f_{\text{count}}(y\mid\mu_i).
$$

Both processes can thus generate an observed zero. A linguistic analysis needs a mechanism that makes some cells structurally unable to occur before it interprets $\omega_i$.

```{r}
#| label: compare-zero-probabilities
#| echo: true
poisson_fit <- glm(truncated_frequency_proxy ~ liaison + final_consonant,
                   poisson(), storme)
nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(truncated_frequency_proxy ~ liaison + final_consonant,
                       data = storme, control = glm.control(maxit = 100L))
storme$observed_zero <- storme$truncated_frequency_proxy == 0L
storme$poisson_zero <- dpois(0L, fitted(poisson_fit))
storme$nb_zero <- dnbinom(0L, size = nb_fit$theta, mu = fitted(nb_fit))
zeros <- aggregate(cbind(observed_zero, poisson_zero, nb_zero) ~ liaison,
                   storme, mean)
zeros
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-zero-comparison
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
zero_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Observed", value = zeros$observed_zero),
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Poisson", value = zeros$poisson_zero),
  data.frame(liaison = zeros$liaison, model = "Negative binomial", value = zeros$nb_zero)
)
zero_long$model <- factor(zero_long$model,
                          levels = c("Observed", "Poisson", "Negative binomial"))
ggplot(zero_long, aes(model, value, shape = liaison)) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = .35), size = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Probability of a zero", shape = NULL) +
  theme_classic()
```

The Poisson stress test assigns almost no zero mass, while the negative-binomial
stress test moves toward the observed proportions without a structural-zero
component. We thus do not fit a zero-inflated model here. Such a model would need
a linguistically motivated process that makes some morpheme cells deterministically
absent, together with a defensible observation model for the positive frequency
measure.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Why is the truncated frequency proxy not a direct token tally?
2. Which two components of a zero-inflated model can produce zero?
3. Why does extra-Poisson zero mass not prove a structural-zero process?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. It is a truncated transformation of summed frequency-per-million values. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. The structural component and the ordinary count component can both produce zero. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. Unmodeled heterogeneity or a negative-binomial count process can also increase zero probability. The mixture needs an independently motivated state. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

The [next page](negative-binomial-regression.qmd) derives that heterogeneous count model.
